scenario.title: Three weeks to submit
scenario.intro: You lead an applied agronomy team in Kenya. An investor has invited a USD 300,000 proposal on conservation agriculture packages across two counties, two seasons, and the deadline is in three weeks. The concept note has to go through the MEAL team, and you need three answers fast: how is this project classified in the MEAL Matrix, how much MEAL budget goes in the proposal, and who does what once the project is awarded. This module gives you those answers and the rules behind them.

objectives.text: Classify a proposal with the MEAL Matrix: pick the project type to find its default M&E complexity, and set the scale from budget and duration.
Apply the adjustment rule to a project's complexity level, and name who confirms the classification, who decides KPI method exceptions and who endorses the annual review.
Compute the base MEAL budget for Small, Medium and MEGA projects from the section 5.10 rules, including the percentage and the floor for Medium projects.
Describe the division of responsibility, the three governance rules and the MEAL team structure: three layers, three pillars, Regional MEAL Leads and Project MEAL Focal Points.
Read the six lifecycle phases, their gates and the RACI, and list the eight elements of the minimum MEAL package every project leaves inception with.
State the rollout milestones and their dates, the two entry points, the five enabling conditions and the operating cadence.

beats.hook: When does MEAL start on your project? If your answer is "at inception" you are already one phase late. The framework puts MEAL into the proposal, before indicators, budgets and data systems are fixed.

example.title: Put the six phases in order
example.prompt: Arrange the six lifecycle phases from the first to the last. Each one ends with a gate that must be passed before the next begins.

items.label: Opportunity and proposal
items.detail: Gate: MEAL section, KPI crosswalk, indicative data architecture and costed MEAL budget before submission.

items.label: Award and inception
items.detail: Gate: approved MEAL plan and measurement matrix within the inception period.

items.label: System and protocol design
items.detail: Gate: data collection system tested; protocols, roles, consent and QA procedures approved.

items.label: Enable and hand over
items.detail: Gate: competency check, live system and named data and MEAL owners.

items.label: Implementation and adaptive management
items.detail: Gate: quarterly or seasonal evidence review with actions, owners and follow-up.

items.label: Outcome, impact, synthesis and learning
items.detail: Gate: validated outcome or impact dataset, institutional KPI update and an evidence product or learning note.

example.why: The lifecycle runs from proposal to impact. Central MEAL is heaviest at the start (design, classification, costing) and at the end (integration from outcomes upward). In the middle, the project runs routine monitoring and central MEAL assures quality and supports outcome measurement.

bullets: Six phases, six gates. The first gate is passed before the proposal is submitted: MEAL section, KPI crosswalk, indicative data architecture and costed MEAL budget.
The RACI gives each activity one accountable role. The project lead is accountable for routine data collection; the Focal Point is responsible for doing it.
For Small projects taking the standard package, the Regional MEAL Lead's Phase 1 role is limited to confirming the classification and the base budget.

lessons.title: The MEAL Matrix: classify your project

beats.hook: Your proposal is applied agronomy, USD 300,000, two years, Kenya. Two choices in the Matrix turn that sentence into a MEAL support package, a KPI list, a set of deliverables and a budget line.

example.title: Classify three proposals
example.prompt: Pick the project type first. It sets the default M&E complexity. Then set the scale from budget and duration. Try the Kenya proposal (applied agronomy, USD 300,000, two years), then a USD 150,000 one-year seed multiplication pilot in Mexico, then a USD 2.5 million three-year digital advisory programme in South Asia. Note what the Matrix returns for each.

bullets: Rows are the six project types. Each type carries a default complexity: Standard for upstream discovery; Intermediate for breeding and for digital agriculture; Complex for applied agronomy, seed systems and system change.

Columns are the four scales: Small up to about USD 280,000 and about one year; Medium about USD 280,000 to 800,000 and 1.5 to 3 years; Large above USD 800,000 up to USD 10 million; MEGA above USD 10 million.
The budget sets the scale, not the complexity. The Regional MEAL Lead confirms the classification at proposal review.

beats.hook: The default complexity is a starting point. Three commitments move a project up one level. And when a project cannot follow a KPI method, somebody specific has to say yes.

example.title: Two proposals, one adjustment
body: A digital advisory proposal in South Asia starts at Intermediate, the default for digital agriculture and AI. Then the team reads the investor's call. It asks for household-level evidence that farmers changed their sowing date after using the advice. The team commits to it. That is the first trigger in the adjustment rule: reporting farmer- or household-level adoption, outcomes or impact to investors. The project moves up one level to Complex. Its Medium budget rule moves with it: 5% instead of 4%, with a floor of USD 18,000 instead of USD 13,000. The scale does not change. It is still a Medium project.

The other two triggers work the same way. A breeding project that runs its own ground measurement of outcomes moves from Intermediate to Complex. An upstream discovery project that depends on primary data from several implementing partners moves from Standard to Intermediate. The Matrix names one move up and three levels, so start reading the rule from Standard or Intermediate.

Who confirms the result? The Regional MEAL Lead, at proposal review. The project lead proposes the type and scale in the Matrix and is responsible for the classification; the Regional MEAL Lead is accountable for it.

Now the exception. The Kenya team wants to estimate yield from farmer recall instead of the crop cuts the KPI reference sheet requires. That is a KPI method exception. Pillar A, Design, Standards and Enablement, works it through; the MEAL Group Lead is accountable for the decision. Neither the project lead nor the Regional MEAL Lead can grant it. Once a year, the MEAL Review Committee, a body at the level of CIMMYT's scientific leadership, reviews the Handbook, the Toolbox and the Matrix and endorses the changes for the following year. The MEAL Group Lead prepares and presents that review.

bullets: Three triggers move a project up one complexity level: committing to report farmer- or household-level adoption, outcomes or impact to investors; running its own ground measurement of outcomes; depending on primary data from several implementing partners.
The adjustment changes complexity, never scale. The Regional MEAL Lead confirms the classification at proposal review.
KPI method exceptions sit with the MEAL Group Lead. The annual review of the Handbook, Toolbox and Matrix is endorsed by the MEAL Review Committee.

beats.hook: Five percent of USD 300,000 is USD 15,000. Is that your MEAL line? Not quite. The Medium rule has a second half, and skipping it is the most common budgeting mistake in the Matrix.

example.title: Run the Kenya calculation, then two more
example.prompt: Start with the Kenya proposal: applied agronomy, so Complex by default; USD 300,000 over two years, so Medium. The Medium rule for Complex is 5% of the total project budget: 5% of USD 300,000 is USD 15,000. Now the second half of the rule: never less than the Small amount for the same complexity level. The Small Complex amount is USD 18,000. USD 15,000 is below it, so the floor applies and the base MEAL budget is USD 18,000. Confirm it with the MEAL team while you write the proposal. Then try a USD 500,000 seed systems project (5% is USD 25,000, above the floor) and a USD 290,000 breeding project (4% is USD 11,600, below the USD 13,000 floor). Finish with a Small digital pilot and a MEGA programme to see the fixed amount and the per-year institutional contribution.

bullets: Small: USD 8,000 Standard, USD 13,000 Intermediate, USD 18,000 Complex, per project for its lifetime. Medium: 3%, 4% or 5% of the total project budget, never less than the Small amount for the same complexity level, confirmed with MEAL during proposal writing.

Large and MEGA are co-designed with MEAL from the start of proposal development. MEGA also carries an institutional contribution of at least USD 27,000 per project year, charged as Core Layer staff time.
The base contribution buys the institutional services every project receives. It funds the eight-element minimum package, and none of those elements waits for end-of-project reporting.

beats.hook: Your base contribution is in. Does that mean central MEAL now runs your monitoring? No. The operating principle is central standards, distributed implementation, institutional integration.

example.title: Who owns what on the Kenya project
body: Processes and outputs. Your team keeps the workplan, the demonstration plot records, the training logs and the partner records. Central MEAL gives you standards, KPI definitions, deduplication and aggregation rules and quality assurance. It does not collect your plot data.

Outcomes. Shared. Your team collects the adoption follow-up with the enumerators you budgeted; central MEAL designs the outcome method, supports sampling and heterogeneity analysis and integrates your records with other projects in the region.
Impact. Central MEAL with science and evaluation specialists. You provide source data and context: who received the package, where and when, plus the implementation history.

If you want central MEAL to run routine monitoring, a baseline survey or a dashboard for you, that is an extended service, charged at cost on top of the base contribution. The base contribution pays for standards, proposal review, quality assurance, integration into the MEAL data system, portfolio reporting and PRMS and investor reporting.

Three rules keep this coherent as the portfolio grows. One: no institutional KPI is added or redefined without MEAL team review, and your project-specific indicators stay project-specific until Pillar A approves them. Two: every proposal goes through the MEAL team at proposal stage, where the Matrix sets scale and complexity. Three: the MEAL Group Lead decides exceptions and the MEAL Review Committee endorses the annual changes.

bullets: Projects own process and output evidence. Outcomes are shared. Impact sits with central MEAL and specialists, with projects supplying source data and context.
The base contribution pays for institutional services, not for running your monitoring. Monitoring, surveys, studies and dashboards run by the MEAL team are extended services charged at cost.

Three governance rules: Toolbox changes need MEAL review and Pillar A approval; every proposal goes through MEAL at proposal stage; the Group Lead decides exceptions and the Review Committee endorses the annual review.

lessons.title: Governance, team structure and how the roles work together

beats.hook: Thirteen positions in two layers, plus a Focal Point in every major project. Who do you call when your crosswalk is stuck, your data dictionary needs a field, or your evaluation needs a design?

example.title: Who owns this task?
example.prompt: Each task has one owner. Drop it on the role that owns it: Pillar A (Design, Standards and Enablement), Pillar B (Evidence Systems and Portfolio Performance), Pillar C (Evaluation, Learning and Accountability), the Regional MEAL Lead, the Project MEAL Focal Point or the Data Group.

bins.hint: Main interface between projects and the Core Layer; one per region.

cards.why: The Portfolio Performance and Visualization Analyst in Pillar B prepares performance packs and maintains the evidence-gap register.

cards.why: The MEAL Measurement Specialist in Pillar A develops reference sheets and indicator crosswalks.

cards.why: The Evaluation and Research Analyst in Pillar C keeps the decision and management-response log.

cards.why: Regional MEAL Leads coach Focal Points, guide their technical work and escalate to the relevant pillar.

cards.why: Maintaining the project MEAL plan and preparing indicator evidence for project, investor and institutional reporting are Focal Point responsibilities.

bullets: Three layers: the Core Layer (MEAL Group Lead plus three pillars, ten positions), the Regional Layer (one Regional MEAL Lead per region: Latin America, Africa, South Asia) and the Project Layer (the Extended MEAL Network of Focal Points). Thirteen positions in Core and Regional Layers.

Handoffs are explicit: Pillar A defines what to measure and the valid method; Pillar B structures, assures, aggregates and visualises the evidence; Pillar C answers questions monitoring cannot and closes the loop to action.

Regional MEAL Leads report to the Group Lead and draw on all three pillars. Focal Points are embedded in and funded by major projects. Geospatial, software and data-science capacity comes from CIMMYT's technical functions, not from inside MEAL.

beats.hook: The Handbook is finalised in September 2026 and every new proposal uses it from October. Your Kenya proposal lands in that window. Here is what has to be in place around it, and what keeps the system alive afterwards.

example.title: Where the Kenya proposal sits on the roadmap
body: May to September 2026 is design and build: the Handbook and the 13 KPI volumes under the three Thrusts, methods and aggregation rules, and the minimum package. In September 2026 the Handbook and KPI Toolbox are finalised and ready for peer validation. In early October 2026 the Senior Leadership Team launches them in a global webinar. From October 12, 2026 regional training starts, and that is where Project MEAL Focal Points and country-level MEAL contacts are identified.

From October 2026, all new proposals use the Toolbox and the guidance. That is your entry point. At concept-note stage the proposal goes through the MEAL team using the Matrix: you select the project type and scale, and the Matrix returns the MEAL support, the applicable KPIs, the expected deliverables and the base budget. Budget for data collection, quality assurance, analysis and learning, not only for reporting.

A sister project in your region, awarded in 2025 with three years still to run, has a different entry point. From November 2026, ongoing projects with more than two years of implementation remaining can pilot the KPI system. The Matrix alone is not enough for them: MEAL runs a readiness diagnostic of existing indicators, systems and gaps against the Handbook, a selection check on remaining duration, budget flexibility, data-system maturity and team capacity, and, for confirmed pilots, a crosswalk workshop that maps existing indicators onto the Toolbox. From 2027 to 2030 the system scales across the portfolio, starting with the first institutional KPI run, a baseline portfolio dashboard and the evidence-gap register.

Five conditions decide whether the roadmap works: strong data systems built with the Data Group; clear roles and governance; quality and accountability embedded through the lifecycle; capacity development through role-based training, communities of practice and office hours; and continuous learning, with improvements released as new versions of the guidance. Once your project runs, it runs on the cadence in 5.7: continuous or monthly quality checks, a quarterly or seasonal evidence review that ends in a decision log, an annual KPI recomputation with a portfolio dashboard and evidence-gap register, and midterm, endline or trigger-based studies.

bullets: Milestones: design and build May to September 2026; Handbook and Toolbox finalised September 2026; launch webinar early October 2026; regional training from October 12, 2026; all new proposals from October 2026; pilots from November 2026; scale 2027 to 2030.

Two entry points: new proposals go through the MEAL team at concept-note stage using the Matrix; ongoing projects with more than two years left join through a readiness diagnostic, a selection check and a crosswalk workshop.

Five enabling conditions: strong data systems, clear roles and governance, quality and accountability, capacity development, continuous learning and adaptation. Then a cadence of monthly checks, quarterly reviews, an annual KPI run and trigger-based studies.

frames.narration: The Matrix is a grid. Six project types down the side, each with a default complexity. Four scales across the top, set by budget and duration. Every cell holds the support, the KPIs, the deliverables and the base budget.
Start small. A one-year demonstration-plot pilot at USD 150,000 is applied agronomy, so Complex by default, and Small by scale. The base budget is fixed: USD 18,000 for the life of the project.

Now the Kenya proposal: USD 300,000 over two years. Same row, one column to the right: Medium. The rule is 5% of the total budget, which is USD 15,000. But never less than the Small amount for the same complexity. USD 18,000 is the floor, so the counter stays at USD 18,000.

Above USD 800,000 the counter stops. Large and MEGA projects co-design MEAL with the team from the start of proposal development. MEGA adds an institutional contribution of at least USD 27,000 per project year, charged as Core Layer staff time.

misconceptions.description: You let the budget, the duration or the number of countries set the complexity level, or you mixed up the two axes of the Matrix. The project type sets the default M&E complexity; budget and duration set the scale.

You applied the Medium percentage or the Small minimum on its own. The Medium rule needs both: take 3%, 4% or 5% of the total budget, then check that it is never less than the Small amount for the same complexity level.

You treated Large or MEGA projects as if they had a fixed amount or a percentage. Above USD 800,000 the MEAL budget is co-designed with the team from the start of proposal development; MEGA adds at least USD 27,000 per project year.

You left MEAL design, classification or budgeting until after the award. The first gate is passed before submission, and from October 2026 every proposal goes through the MEAL team at concept-note stage.

You handed routine project monitoring to the central MEAL team. Projects own process and output evidence and first-line quality checks; the centre sets standards, assures quality and integrates from outcomes upward.

You let a project add or redefine an institutional KPI on its own. Projects can add project-specific indicators, but nothing becomes institutional without MEAL review and approval by the Design, Standards and Enablement pillar.

You gave the project lead, the Regional MEAL Lead or a pillar the final say on a KPI method exception or on the annual review. The MEAL Group Lead is accountable for exceptions; the MEAL Review Committee endorses the annual changes.

Intermediate complexity, Medium scale
Complex complexity, Medium scale

questions.explanation: Seed systems and deployment carries Complex as its default complexity, and USD 150,000 over about one year is Small. The modest budget changes the scale, not the complexity.
questions.reviewTip: Read the project type row first, then the scale column.

questions.question: A digital advisory programme in South Asia has a USD 2.5 million budget over three years in two countries. What are its scale and default complexity?

options.text: MEGA scale, Complex complexity
Medium scale, Intermediate complexity
Large scale, Complex complexity
Large scale, Intermediate complexity

questions.explanation: Above USD 800,000 and up to USD 10 million is Large, and digital agriculture and AI defaults to Intermediate. Multi-country work does not make a project MEGA; MEGA starts above USD 10 million.
questions.reviewTip: Check the scale thresholds in the column headers of Annex A.

questions.question: Which commitment triggers the Matrix adjustment rule and moves a project up one complexity level?

options.text: Reporting to the investor every quarter instead of once a year
Reporting farmer- or household-level adoption to the investor
Working in three countries instead of one
Having a total budget above USD 800,000

questions.explanation: The three triggers are committing to report farmer- or household-level adoption, outcomes or impact to investors, running the project's own ground measurement of outcomes, and depending on primary data from several implementing partners. Budget and country count affect scale, not complexity.
questions.reviewTip: Read the adjustment rule in Annex A and list its three triggers.

questions.question: Who confirms a project's Matrix classification at proposal review?

options.text: The MEAL Review Committee
The project lead
The Regional MEAL Lead
The Data Group

questions.explanation: Annex A states that the Regional MEAL Lead confirms the classification at proposal review, and the RACI gives the Regional MEAL Lead the A for that activity. The project lead is responsible for proposing it, not for confirming it.
questions.reviewTip: Read the first RACI row under Phase 1.

questions.question: An upstream discovery project with a USD 400,000 budget over two years stays at its default Standard complexity. What is its base MEAL budget?

options.text: USD 12,000, because 3% of USD 400,000 is above the USD 8,000 floor
USD 8,000, because Standard projects always pay the Small amount
USD 16,000, because Medium projects use the 4% rate
USD 20,000, because Medium projects use the 5% rate

questions.explanation: USD 400,000 over two years is Medium, and the Medium Standard rate is 3%, which gives USD 12,000. That is above the USD 8,000 Small Standard floor, so the percentage stands.
questions.reviewTip: Match the percentage to the complexity level, then compare with the Small amount for that level.

questions.question: A multi-environment breeding project has a USD 500,000 budget over three years at its default Intermediate complexity. What base MEAL budget applies?

options.text: USD 13,000, the Small Intermediate amount
USD 15,000, which is 3% of the budget
USD 25,000, which is 5% of the budget
USD 20,000, which is 4% of the budget

questions.explanation: The Medium Intermediate rate is 4%, and 4% of USD 500,000 is USD 20,000. That is above the USD 13,000 floor, so USD 20,000 applies; the floor only steps in when the percentage falls below it.
questions.reviewTip: Use the Medium row of the base budget table: 3%, 4% or 5% by complexity level.

questions.question: Which phrase states the operating principle behind the division of responsibility?

options.text: Central collection, central analysis, central reporting
Central standards, distributed implementation, institutional integration
Project standards, project implementation, project reporting
Regional standards, regional implementation, regional integration

questions.explanation: Section 5.2 states the principle as central standards, distributed implementation, institutional integration. Projects generate the evidence closest to delivery; central MEAL makes sure it supports comparable outcome and impact analysis.

source.title: Division of Responsibility: Project Delivery vs. Institutional MEAL

questions.reviewTip: Read the first paragraph of section 5.2.

questions.question: How are Regional MEAL Leads placed in the team structure?

options.text: One per project, reporting to the Project MEAL Focal Point
One per pillar, reporting to that pillar's Senior Lead
One per region, reporting to the MEAL Group Lead and drawing on all three pillars
One per country, reporting to the Data Group

questions.explanation: There is one Regional MEAL Lead in each of the three regions: Latin America, Africa and South Asia. They report directly to the MEAL Group Lead and draw on all three pillars instead of sitting under one of them.
questions.reviewTip: Read the Regional Layer paragraph in section 5.8.

questions.question: What happens in early October 2026, before regional training starts on October 12?

options.text: The Senior Leadership Team launches the Handbook and Toolbox in a global webinar
The first institutional KPI run produces the baseline portfolio dashboard
Ongoing projects are confirmed as pilots after a readiness diagnostic
The MEAL Review Committee endorses the first annual changes to the Matrix

questions.explanation: Milestone 3 is the launch webinar in early October 2026, led by the Senior Leadership Team before regional training begins. Pilots start from November 2026 and the first KPI run belongs to the 2027 to 2030 scale phase.
questions.reviewTip: Put the seven milestones on a timeline and check the dates.

questions.question: An applied agronomy proposal in Kenya has a USD 300,000 budget over two years in two counties. How does the Matrix classify it by default?

options.text: Intermediate complexity, Medium scale, because the budget is modest
Complex complexity, Small scale, because it runs in one country
Complex complexity, Medium scale
Standard complexity, Medium scale, because it is a two-year pilot

questions.explanation: Applied agronomy and farming systems defaults to Complex, and USD 300,000 over two years falls in the Medium band of about USD 280,000 to 800,000 and 1.5 to 3 years. Budget and duration set the scale; the project type sets the complexity.
questions.reviewTip: Classify in two steps: type gives complexity, then budget and duration give scale.

questions.question: A breeding acceleration programme has a USD 900,000 budget over four years in three countries. What does the Matrix return?

options.text: Large scale, Intermediate complexity by default
MEGA scale, because it is multi-country and multi-year
Large scale, Complex complexity, because Large projects are always Complex
Medium scale, Intermediate complexity, because it runs under USD 1 million

questions.explanation: Above USD 800,000 and up to USD 10 million is Large, and breeding and varietal development defaults to Intermediate. Scale does not raise complexity; only the adjustment rule's three triggers do.
questions.reviewTip: Keep the two axes separate: scale from the column headers, complexity from the row.

questions.question: A Medium digital advisory project at Intermediate complexity will depend on primary data from four implementing partners. What does the adjustment rule require?

options.text: It stays Intermediate, because the project type fixes the level
It moves up one level to Complex, and stays Medium
It moves up to Large scale, because more partners mean more reach
It moves only if the project lead agrees to the higher budget

questions.explanation: Depending on primary data from several implementing partners is one of the three triggers, so the project moves up one complexity level to Complex. Scale is unchanged, and the Regional MEAL Lead confirms the classification rather than the project lead choosing it.
questions.reviewTip: Check the three triggers; partner data dependence is the third.

questions.question: A wheat project in South Asia wants to estimate yield from farmer recall instead of the crop cuts the KPI reference sheet requires. Who is accountable for granting that exception?

options.text: The project lead, because the project owns its output evidence
The Regional MEAL Lead, because the region reviews proposals
The Data Group, because it owns the data system
The MEAL Group Lead, with Pillar A responsible for the work

questions.explanation: Governance rule 3 makes the MEAL Group Lead accountable for exceptions to KPI methods, and the RACI row for KPI method exceptions gives R to Pillar A and A to the Group Lead. The project lead and Regional MEAL Lead are consulted, not deciding.
questions.reviewTip: Read governance rule 3 and the KPI method exceptions row of the RACI.

questions.question: A regional seed deployment project has a USD 500,000 budget over three years and confirmed Complex complexity. What is its base MEAL budget?

options.text: USD 18,000, the Complex minimum, because Medium Complex projects always pay the floor
USD 15,000, which is 3% of the budget
USD 25,000, which is 5% of the budget and above the floor
USD 20,000, which is 4% of the budget

questions.explanation: The Medium Complex rate is 5%, and 5% of USD 500,000 is USD 25,000, which is above the USD 18,000 Small Complex amount. The floor only replaces the percentage when the percentage is lower.
questions.reviewTip: Compute the percentage, then take the larger of that and the Small amount.

questions.question: A breeding project has a USD 290,000 budget over 18 months at Intermediate complexity. What base MEAL budget applies?

options.text: USD 11,600, which is 4% of the budget
USD 8,700, which is 3% of the budget
USD 13,000, because 4% falls below the Small Intermediate amount
USD 18,000, because any Medium project pays the highest floor

questions.explanation: USD 290,000 over 18 months is Medium, and 4% of it is USD 11,600, which is below the USD 13,000 Small Intermediate amount, so the floor applies. The floor is the Small amount for the same complexity level, not the highest Small amount.
questions.reviewTip: The phrase to remember is: never less than the Small amount for the same complexity level.

questions.question: A multi-country applied agronomy programme has a USD 3 million budget over four years. How is its MEAL budget set?

options.text: Co-designed with the MEAL team from the start of proposal development
At 5% of the total budget, which is USD 150,000
At the fixed USD 18,000 Complex amount for the project lifetime
Agreed with the MEAL team after the award, during inception

questions.explanation: Above USD 800,000 and up to USD 10 million is Large, and the table says Large budgets are co-designed with MEAL from the start of proposal development. There is no percentage or fixed amount for Large projects in section 5.10.
questions.reviewTip: Read the Large row of the base budget table.

questions.question: A MEGA proposal of USD 12 million over five years budgets USD 27,000 in total for institutional MEAL. What is wrong?

options.text: Nothing, USD 27,000 is the fixed MEGA amount
It should be 5% of the budget instead
It should be USD 18,000, the highest fixed amount
The USD 27,000 is a minimum per project year, on top of project-specific MEAL work

questions.explanation: MEGA budgets are co-designed and cover project-specific MEAL work plus an institutional contribution, charged as Core Layer staff time, of at least USD 27,000 per project year. Over five years that contribution alone is at least USD 135,000.
questions.reviewTip: Read the MEGA row and note the words per project year.

questions.question: A project lead in Kenya asks the central MEAL team to run the project's routine output monitoring, arguing the base contribution already pays for it. What does the framework say?

options.text: Yes, routine monitoring is an institutional service covered by the base contribution
No, routine monitoring stays with the project; the team can run it as an extended service charged at cost
Yes, once the project is classified as Complex the centre takes over data collection
No, routine monitoring is the Regional MEAL Lead's job

questions.explanation: The base contribution pays for standards, proposal review, quality assurance, integration and portfolio and investor reporting, and project teams remain responsible for routine monitoring. Running project monitoring is listed among the extended services charged at cost.
questions.reviewTip: Compare what the base contribution buys with the extended services list in 5.10.

questions.question: A project wants to redefine the institutional yield KPI so that it matches the investor's template. What does governance rule 1 require?

options.text: The project may redefine it locally as long as the investor agrees
The Regional MEAL Lead can approve the new definition for the region
No KPI is redefined without MEAL team review; approved changes appear in a new Handbook version
The Data Group updates the KPI engine to the investor definition

questions.explanation: Rule 1 says no institutional KPI is added or redefined without review by the MEAL team, and approved changes are published in a new version of the Handbook. The project can report the investor measure through the crosswalk without touching the institutional definition.
questions.reviewTip: Read governance rule 1 and the crosswalk element of the minimum package.

questions.question: How are Project MEAL Focal Points positioned in the structure?

options.text: Embedded in and funded by major projects, applying institutional standards with guidance from the Regional MEAL Lead
Counted among the thirteen Core and Regional positions and funded centrally
Hired by the Core Layer to run project monitoring from headquarters
Placed under Pillar B to maintain the institutional data dictionary

questions.explanation: Focal Points form the Extended MEAL Network; they are embedded in and funded by major projects and receive technical guidance from their Regional MEAL Lead. The thirteen positions are the Core and Regional Layers only.
questions.reviewTip: Read the Project Layer paragraph in section 5.8.

questions.question: A project leaves inception with a results chain, a crosswalk and a measurement plan, and plans to add the baseline and the learning calendar at the endline. Is that acceptable?

options.text: Yes, the baseline can be reconstructed from recall at the endline
No, all eight package elements are in place at inception; none is left to end-of-project reporting
Yes, Small projects only need the first three elements
No, but only the baseline is mandatory; the learning calendar is optional

questions.explanation: Section 5.4 lists eight elements every project leaves inception with, including a baseline or documented alternative and a learning and accountability cycle. Depth varies by scale, but none of the elements is left to end-of-project reporting.
questions.reviewTip: Count the eight elements and check each against your inception plan.

questions.question: Which list names the five enabling conditions in section 5.6?

options.text: Investor compliance, annual reporting, central monitoring, audits, dashboards
Strong data systems, clear roles and governance, quality and accountability, capacity development, continuous learning and adaptation
Bridge funding, new hires, software licences, consultants, regional offices
Theory of change, crosswalk, measurement plan, baseline, handover

questions.explanation: The five conditions are strong data systems, clear roles and governance, quality and accountability, capacity development, and continuous learning and adaptation. Option d lists elements of the minimum package, not enabling conditions.
questions.reviewTip: Read the five boxes in section 5.6.

questions.question: A concept note is due in December 2026. What is the entry point for new proposals on the roadmap?

options.text: MEAL joins at inception, after the award, to build the plan
A readiness diagnostic and a selection check on remaining duration
The investor's template sets the indicators; MEAL maps them later
The proposal goes through the MEAL team at concept-note stage using the Matrix

questions.explanation: From October 2026 every proposal goes through the MEAL team at concept-note stage using the MEAL Matrix, which returns support, KPIs, deliverables and base budget. The readiness diagnostic and selection check are the entry point for ongoing projects joining as pilots.
questions.reviewTip: Compare the entry points under milestones 5 and 6.

questions.question: On the operating cadence, what does a quarterly or seasonal evidence review produce?

options.text: A portfolio dashboard and the evidence-gap register
Quality flags and a system issue log
A decision log: what changes, who acts, by when
Evaluation findings and an updated impact narrative

questions.explanation: The quarterly or seasonal review is a joint look at implementation, reach, early uptake and emerging outcomes, and its output is a decision log. Quality flags come from monthly checks, the dashboard and gap register from the annual run, and evaluation findings from trigger-based studies.
questions.reviewTip: Match each cadence row to its typical output in the 5.7 table.

glossaryAdditions.definition: The size band of a project in the MEAL Matrix, set by budget and duration: Small (up to about USD 280,000, around one year), Medium (about USD 280,000 to 800,000, 1.5 to 3 years), Large (above USD 800,000 up to USD 10 million) or MEGA (above USD 10 million).
Senior leader of the institutional MEAL function. Accountable for Handbook changes and KPI method exceptions, and prepares and presents the annual review to the MEAL Review Committee.
The Project Layer of the MEAL structure: Project MEAL Focal Points embedded in and funded by major projects, applying institutional standards with guidance from their Regional MEAL Lead.
